text: A script that only runs when someone opens a terminal on their own laptop has three real problems, and none of them are about whether the script's logic is correct. Where and how a script runs turns out to matter just as much as what it actually does once it runs.

First, there's no record of who ran it, when, or what happened — if it quietly stops running for two weeks because someone was on vacation, nobody finds out until something downstream breaks. Second, it breaks the moment that one laptop is in for repair, reimaged, or just turned off; the automation isn't really automated, it's one person remembering to run a command. Third, environments drift: one machine has a newer PowerShell and module version than another, so the same script can behave differently for reasons that have nothing to do with the script itself.

A real CI/CD pipeline — GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps Pipelines — runs the script on a managed, hosted machine instead, and fixes all three problems directly. The pipeline definition specifies exactly which runner image and which module versions get installed, so every run gets an identical environment regardless of whose commit triggered it. Every run is logged automatically: the commit, the timestamp, the full console output, visible later to anyone on the team.

A pipeline can also be triggered reliably — on a schedule using a cron expression, on every push to a branch, or on demand with a manual button — firing exactly when it's configured to, with no dependency on a specific person being at their desk. cron: "0 7 * * MON-FRI" fires a job at 07:00 UTC every weekday; workflow_dispatch adds a button to run it manually whenever needed.

runs-on: ubuntu-latest picks a hosted runner with a known, consistent image, the same one every single run uses — which is the entire point of moving a script off a laptop and into a pipeline. Next up: how that same pipeline authenticates to Azure or AWS safely, without ever putting a secret into the repository itself.
